It says here verbatim, "defence liberating unit conducting the combat." So the Osmace unit was a part of the Srebrenica TO Staff, and the commander of that TO staff was Brigadier Naser Oric. So I could say that you were right, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. In fact to make progress through these forms I would be grateful if where possible you would answer with simply a yes or no, and I take it you've answered my question yes, the form does not say that Oric planned the attack. My next question is, it does not say either that Naser Oric participated in the attack, does it? And again, please, a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As you've explained it simply says that according to this draft, this form, Osmace TO came within the formation of the Srebrenica TO Staff and you've explained that might be at some later stage. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, the unit -- paragraph 4 states that the liberation unit -- I know this is not the correct translation but it says that the liberation unit in charge of the operation during its execution and the commander is Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes that's my point and this can be taken in re-examination. If I may, the witness agreed with the last sheet that in fact it might record that a unit was within the Srebrenica TO Staff event though it wasn't at the time of the combat operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'm putting it to the witness that that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead, Mr. Jones, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've accepted the possibility that even though these forms state that a unit is within the Srebrenica TO Staff it might be that they later came within the staff and were not so at the time of the combat operations?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Or perhaps they acted together in the course of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now again if you could just answer the following questions with a yes or no, if possible. According to paragraph 4, Naser Oric had no rank during the combat operations, correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now on Friday, you described Naser Oric on several occasions as Brigadier Oric. He didn't in fact become a brigadier until July 1994, did he?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I assume that you're right because approximately at around that time, all of us were promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now if you look at paragraph 8 of this sheet, do you agree that it sets out there a military objective for the combat operation, namely to crush enemy forces, extend the free territory and create conditions for further defence of the country, cut the linking of Chetnik units along Fakovici, Ratkovici, Brezani? Ratkovici didn't enter the record. Ratkovici, Fakovici, Brezani. You see that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you understand, then, from this document that at least from the 19th of June 1992, there were Chetnik units, or in other words Serb military forces, deployed and linked together in Fakovici, Ratkovici, and Brezani?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you'd also understand from this form, wouldn't you, that the combat action had the task of seizing as much materiel and technical equipment and supplies as well as food, in other words war booty, and of killing the enemy. That's in paragraph 8(2).

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's what is stated in 8(2).

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: These are all perfectly legitimate military objectives, as far as the regulations you were referring to on Friday were concerned, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this, yes, that's what follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then we see at paragraph 9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I should just explain for Your Honours that in the original various paragraphs are circled and in the English they appear not to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right, General, that we see at paragraph 9 that the operation had tactical importance and according to paragraph 17(3), in fact, had great tactical importance compared with other actions carried out by those units. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 13, it appears that units involved in this action used a white band around their head to distinguish each other. Now, would you understand from that, that fighters, persons properly engaged in this action, wore white bands around their head?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When it comes to members of the then Territorial Defence. The band around the head or around the arm was a way to make a distinction between us and enemy soldiers. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because at the time there were very few uniforms, correct, so there had to be a way of recognising one's fellow combatant?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely so. That was the case almost throughout 1992, because both sides had almost identical uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it follows from this form, doesn't it, that a person not wearing a white band was not a participant in these operations, as far as this is concerned?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those who were in battlefield and took part in combat and did not have the bands, either around the head or around the arm, were considered to be enemy soldiers and as such were targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And if this form is accurate in any respect, it's correct to say, isn't it, that looking at paragraph 20.7, a number of light weapons and some heavy weapons, from a 60-millimetre mortar and two 82 millimetre mortars were captured from the enemy Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't think we are referring to the same item or section. Could you please repeat your question because the text -- my text doesn't say what you read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Paragraph 20.7?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have to turn the page because it seems that 20.7 is repeated twice. Or at least that's how it was understood by whoever translated. You need to refer to the page, General, which at the top, right-hand corner has the following reference number, 02621344. And there you see 20.7, [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's losses suffered by occupying aggressor forces --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I see now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That refers to Serbian forces, doesn't it, "occupying aggressor forces"?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it now. I would like to thank Your Honour for pointing me in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now as someone who was in the armed forces during this period and as someone involved in these forms would you understand from 20.7 that the Serb forces had lost or had captured from them 60-millimetre mortar and two, 82-millimetre mortars, apart from other things, apart from light weapons?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is clear here that they seized not only two mortars of 82-millimetre calibre but as well one piece of 6-0 millimetre mortar, so three mortars altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you're very familiar with this equipment, aren't you? We are talking about heavy weapons which can inflict a lot of damage on people and property within range, correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to P88, which concerns Kravica. This is out of chronological sequence but it's in exhibit sequence so that's why I've taken that order. Now, this concerns an action in Kravica which according to this form began and ended on the 7th of January 1993, according to paragraph 12, correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To see which unit carried out this action we actually need to look at the Bosnian because I think there is a mistake in the English. Would you agree that at 2 it says, first, [B/C/S spoken]?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cerani detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In other words that's the first Cerska [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And according to this document, this was a detachment that was with the Territorial Defence Staff of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's just -- so, for the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So where we have "Cerani" in English, that's a mistake. It should read "Cerska."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Exactly "Ceranski" means "Cerska," as this witness has confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour I've been distracted by e-mails. I apologise. Would you just give me a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I direct to you paragraph 2 in both versions, the English and the B/C/S. If you look at the original, the B/C/S version, paragraph 2, line 1, handwritten you find number 1, [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was translated for us as 1st Cerani detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being suggested and it seems that the witness agrees that Ceranski should never be translated Cerani but it should read Cerska, Cerska, Cerska, 1st Cerska detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, it takes me by surprise. I can't comment because I'm not a native speaker. I think it's probably a matter for the -- for the interpreter's booth or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I will just ask this witness again to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If the witness knows, I don't know if it's idiom or whether in the language you can get Ceranski from Cerska. That's what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is become being unnecessarily complicated. Can I just ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: General, do you understand [B/C/S spoken] to refer to the 1st Cerska detachment?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the same. It is just differently put.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you agreed that this detachment -- well, as stated on this form, comes within the Vlasenica TO, we saw that on P123 as well. And you agree that the Vlasenica TO is obviously a different TO from Srebrenica TO?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the officer who it is stated was most responsible for planning the operation, or the action, was Ferid Hodzic, who as we would expect is the commander of the Vlasenica TO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what it states.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So according to this form, the attack on Kravica village -- sorry, put it this way: It was units in the Vlasenica TO which planned and participated in this action on Kravica on the 7th of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what can be read from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, then we see the familiar box 4, saying which formation the unit was within, and here as we saw rather than referring to Srebrenica TO, it says the joint armed forces of the subregion. My question to you is this: When you were a commander in the TO in Tuzla, or even a 2nd Corps commander, you never heard of any properly formed unit called the joint armed forces of the subregion, did you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Joint armed forces or the forces that participated could have only been formed in 1994 or 1995 when we formed the liberation units by which we would join a couple of corps if necessary to assign some units that could bear a similar name. But as for the armed forces of the subregion, I have never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 9, we see a reference to the Kamenica detachment. Kamenica is in Zvornik municipality, isn't it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again if you can just answer with a yes or no, according to this form, or this form doesn't state that Naser Oric either planned or participated in the attack on Kravica.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again I want to take you to the information listed in other paragraphs, and again if you can confirm the following, firstly paragraph 8, again it appears from this form that there was a military objective for this operation which to summarise involved taking territory to enable contact between the free territories of Srebrenica and Konjevic Polje and to take enemy weapons. Do you see that and do you agree that that's what emerges?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. It is defined in 8.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And again, these are perfectly legitimate military objectives, are they not, as far as the ABiH regulations you referred to on Friday are concerned?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please I'm not objecting, I'm asking for an elucidation. This is the second time that Mr. Jones has asked the witness about ABiH regulations referred to on Friday. I think we should know which particular regulations Mr. Jones and the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We saw, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd have to check the transcript. I was referring in general to the provisions of obeying the laws of war which were referred to the witness. I don't know if I need to be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, it's only for the purposes of any re-examination, if any, and I was particularly concerned about the legitimate material being legitimate war aims. That was in the earlier reference to -- made by Mr. Jones so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, it was partly also the reference to war booty which the witness referred to on Friday. I think without stopping and looking at the transcript on Friday I couldn't be more specific. I can undertake in the next break to have a look, otherwise, I'm happy to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I would appreciate that because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Di Fazio. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again we can take these points quickly. Paragraph 9, apparently the operation had tactical importance. Coupled with 17.3, great tactical importance. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then if we look at the forces engaged, paragraph 18, it says that the enemy were about 500 Chetniks. Would we understand from that that that's referring to 500 members of the Serb military, 500 Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. We made a distinction between Chetniks who were Bosnian Serbs fighting the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the JNA, which actually, as a military formation would come from Serbia to participate in combat activities. When we would say Chetniks, these were formations that were either individually or a part of the larger force who were fighting the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So we are certainly not talking about civilians there?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. There were tens of thousands of Serbs in Tuzla and no one ever called them Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you and you would understand, would you not, from paragraph 18.1.2 that these 500 Serb soldiers had APs, that's machine-guns, Zoljas and, stopping there firstly, you see that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. It also states one tank, one howitzer. So those are heavy -- that's heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Zoljas are incendiary grenades, aren't they, they are grenades which have a propensity to cause fire?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Zolja is an anti-tank device but it could also be used to destroy enemy forces once -- if they were fortified.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. And when we see 20 heavy weapons as well? 18.1, 2, B?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it states here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree, again this is -- well, would you agree that this is a huge amount of weaponry and a very strong opponent considering that on the government side, we are looking at 250 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your assertion is correct. This is a battalion of Chetnik forces, an expanded battalion, rather, and when we are talking -- we are talking about two aggressor companies and in order to fight that unit, the attacking unit should have been at least three times stronger.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that perhaps why at 8.2 we see that the task was to launch surprise attack because in fact they were outnumbered two to one, according to this form, by the Serbs? If you can't comment, don't worry; we can move on.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the only way to see such a task through.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, according to paragraph 20.7, it says "losses suffered by occupying aggressor forces, 60 light weapons, five heavy weapons, and 10.000 pieces of ammunition. Now you would understand this to mean that all these things were captured from the Serbs in the action on the 7th of January 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the Serbs but from the Chetniks, from their armed formations. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So this would appear to have been a very successful military operation, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just on the last subject, your answer concerning Chetniks, is it right on the front page where you see SCA written by hand, on the front page, the first page of this, that refers to Serbia and Montenegrin aggression, SCA?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, when the documents were used, this abbreviation was used for the Serb-Montenegro aggression or aggressor, which I think is more likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that would distinguish these records from, say, sheets relating to combat with the HVO, for example?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you to be right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn to P89 now which is the action sheet relating to Bjelovac, if the witness could be shown that? Now, first, and again for the record, can you confirm that this concerns an action in Bjelovac which apparently started on the 14th of December 1992 and apparently ended on the 18th of December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it states in item 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: From your experience of reviewing these sheets and just your experience generally, would you agree that an action lasting four days would usually mean that it was one that was met with a lot of stiff resistance from the enemy?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That must be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again we can take these points quickly. You've confirmed or the form itself states that the unit in charge was Skenderovici Battalion commanded by Senahid Tabakovic, and it is not stated on this form, is it, that Naser Oric participated in the attack on Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct. Item 2, with all the data contained from 2.1 to 2.9 is precisely what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. It does say, paragraph 3, that Naser Oric was according to this, the officer most responsible for planning the BD, the [B/C/S spoken] combat actions. It also says, doesn't it, at paragraph 3.3, that during the planning, Naser Oric was a member of the Srebrenica military intelligence service, VOS. My question is this: That does not fit, does it, with any information which you have about Naser Oric, that he was in the military intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I don't know whether we are looking at the same material. In my item 3, what is mentioned is the officer most responsible for planning, and then his data.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And then in paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's 3.3 that you have to look, three lines further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 3.3, according to the English translation, Naser Oric was a member of the Srebrenica VOS military intelligence service. Is that -- is that information which you can verify or is it false.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see paragraph 3. I have a rather bad copy and under 3.3 it states "during the planning of the combat activity, the person was a member of Srebrenica," and then there are some letters, I don't know whether that is VOS. It is insufficiently legible for me to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would agree with HIM, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, well, the interpreters have had a stab at it. I can move on from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in 4, we see again this and annotation that according to this draft, the Skenderovici Battalion was, at least at some stage, within the formation of the Srebrenica TO. Now, earlier I asked you about the establishment of corps in September 1992. This draft relates to events in mid-December 1992. And here we are still speak of the Srebrenica TO, not of any unit or did I advice of the ABiH, correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already commented on it and I believe the previous document had the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. So would we understand from this form that in December 1992 in Srebrenica, a TO structure was still in place?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm asking on the basis of there norm which we have in front of us?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the form, yes, but I don't know what the real situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, we can deal with these points quickly. According to this, Naser Oric had no rank during the combat operations?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what one can read from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again if we look at the military objective which is set out in paragraph 8, to summarise, the aim was to crush Serb military forces to liberate Bosniak villages which had been taken by the Serbs. Would you agree that that's a fair summary of 8.1?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it states.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As far as 8.2 is concerned, is the task to seize war booty if I may put it that way, and also important features, in order to prosecute the war effort. My question is, would you understand important features there to refer to, say, hills or other positions of tactical importance?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If those positions were to be seized, that would mean that they were in the hands of the Serb enemy, correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That must be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would you understand from this that in December 1992, Serb military forces were located in the area of combat operations, namely in the Bjelovac area?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally, paragraph 9, would you agree the operation had tactical importance and again according to 17.3, great tactical importance, compared with other actions carried out by those units?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then finally I have -- well, two more subjects on this form. Paragraph 13 we have the reference to the yellow ribbon. You've provided an answer already on this subject. But may I take it then that participants in this action wore yellow ribbons?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the same comment. Your Honour, you should know that those ribbons changed from one action to another and they were never the same and they were never worn in the same place once it would -- it was around the forehead, then on another occasion it would be on the upper arm and on -- or on some other part of the body because we wanted to avoid the possibility of the enemy having the same ribbons in the same place, which could cause great damage or consequences for both sides. That's why we try to change from one action to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. So according to this and according to what you've said if you weren't wearing a white -- wearing a yellow ribbon in Bjelovac, you weren't a participant in the action?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would mean that you didn't belong to that part of the armed formations. Hence, you were an enemy and as such a legitimate target.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or it could mean equally couldn't it, that you were, let's say, a civilian who just happened to be in the area or who had wandered into the area?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. I'm sorry, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's all right. I think your answers are clear. I may come back to it. Now, finally, again because we are short on time, paragraph 20.7 refers to losses suffered by occupying aggressor forces. Would you agree that the Serbs had in fact occupied this area of the combat operations, in other words this area along the Drina, in the area of Bjelovac, Zaluzje, Voljevica, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, if one is to find two tanks in that area that were seized as well as two armoured personnel carriers and four anti-aircraft gun of large calibre, then this is a formidable enemy force. It could not have been a company or even a battalion. It must have been greater. One cannot have a tank and a civilian in one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. It was really also in relation to paragraph 20.3 and 20.5 where we see "liberated temporarily occupied territory, L Rijeka," which I don't think there is no dispute is Loznicka Rijeka, "Bjelovac," Voljevica, I think it should read. Should we understand from that that these are areas which -- in which Bosniaks lived which were occupied by the Serbs and which had been liberated during the course of these -- of this action?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit I don't know that region. I never went there, and I don't know what the ethnic composition was and who lived there. But you could perhaps check the data as to what the population composition was. I would presume there were Bosniaks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as we saw you've signed this form and it's no criticism that you didn't check all the information, but you agree therefore that forms were signed by the commander even without necessarily all the information being checked as accurate?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, at the moment this was put together, maybe they did not have an opportunity to verify, so in my view, this is just a basis, material, or starting point for any consequent analysis. That's why they recorded the names of the people who took or wrote down the data and the revisers. These are the people who should consequently testify on the sources. And it wasn't up to me as a commander to check and verify the data. It was supposed to be done by the team, I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We have two more or two new exhibits which are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just before we live this exhibit I wanted to ask one question with regard to the ranks not mentioned with regard to Naser in number 4, I realise that there are no ranks mentioned also with other -- with regard to other people mentioned here, with one exception, in number 5.1, Mirsad Dudic, second Lieutenant before war. Now, is there some explanation why no ranks are mentioned with regard to these people except a position before the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an explanation, a clearer one, Your Honour. I as commander of the municipal staff and later on as a commander of the operative group was addressed either as commander or as major because in the former JNA I was a major and that was carried on. The orders on appointments and ranks arrived later and depending on the establishment post, and where the commander was, the ranks were appointed. First they were appointed to the people who were in the General Staff, and later on operative groups, brigades, and lower formations. So at the time when these combat operations were conducted, at that time Mr. Naser Oric did not hold a rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact just on that subject according to 3.6 and 3.7, he had no rank before the war either, either as an active officer or as a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's an established fact which is not contested by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes we have these two. We will start with the new document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which new document, because which document are you referring the witness to now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a new document which will be passed up --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- and the ERN number 02621361 to 02621362. And just to explain, it concerns an alleged action in Magasici on the 21st of June 1992, and unfortunately as we discovered these yesterday, we don't have an English translation so I'll just have to ask the witness a few brief questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, do you agree that in concerns -- firstly, do you agree that this is in the same form as the other ones we've seen?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I have seen so far is on the same form, yes. Same document, including this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It concerns an alleged action in Magasici on the 21st of June 1992 as we see from numbers 1 and numbers 12. Now looking at item 2, does it not appear that the unit which conducted the combat operation was a company of the Pale Battalion? I'll ask you that because the "C" in front of the battalion Pale, that refers to Ceta, doesn't it, or does it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. The unit which conducted combat operation was a company from the Pale Battalion. Why it was called Pale, I don't know. Perhaps the battalion was from that town or perhaps from municipality of Pale, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And then if we look at 3, we see that there is the Pale battalion which was involved in planning the operation. Now --

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the same commander who was company commander and who planned combat operations. This is Mr. Smajo Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now we've seen in two of the forms, P87 and P89, that the units were said to be part of the Srebrenica TO. In this draft in paragraph 4 we do not see such an entry, do we? We see that the units participating in the action were only in the Pale Battalion and it's -- that battalion is not said to be part of a greater TO formation, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you. This was an independent battalion that was engaged here which was not within any TO, either Srebrenica or Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number for this document. I think it's D298.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document will become Defence Exhibit D298.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then we can deal rapidly with the next one which is another of these forms. For the record the exhibit number is 02621249 to 02621252 -- sorry, did I say exhibit number? I meant ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would you agree, general, that this concerns an action in Spat, in fact Cela Spat, village Spat?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that it's apparently on the 8th of August? And that's looking at paragraph 12. 8th of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now looking at item 2 it appears that the units which conducted this action was the Srebrenica unit under commander Hakija Meholjic. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it appears in 3, item 3, that he planned the attack, correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that according to 4, that unit, the Srebrenica unit, under Hakija Meholjic was not within any other formation, including the Srebrenica TO?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask for an exhibit number, D299.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become Defence Exhibit D299.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Moving to another area that I think we have 15 minutes still until the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it -- I think we need to move briefly into private session because it's the document we dealt with on Friday in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Jones. Let's move into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You were making comments about a multi-ethnic RBH. In this trial, the Prosecution has repeatedly referred to the Muslim army. I think we need to clarify that. Can you confirm for us that the RBH, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was not a Muslim entity but the government of a sovereign state recognised by the UN and the EU, firstly?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I personally am offended when somebody refers to me as a Muslim or Bosniak commander and soldier. Firstly, I was a Muslim and Bosniak commander and soldier but I was also a commander to everybody else, to the Serbs, Albanians and other ethnic minorities. If I were to tell you that within the first unit that I established in April and May of 1992, I had an almost proportional ethnic makeup in the sabotage reconnaissance unit then it will become clear to you that we wanted to tailor our state to a citizen, meaning not a Bosniak, not a Serb, not a Croat, but we wanted to tailor it to a citizen and that our main orientation was the state within its centuries-old borders. So let me conclude, I'm offended as a person whether somebody refers to me as a "Muslim soldier." I have stated to some of the investigators that I would refuse to speak to them because this is something that offends me and it does not offend me only as a person but also because of others who under the same flag were killed and whose graves are scattered throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know that in a unit, 90 per cent of members were Bosniaks but if there is a single Croat member, then he should also be taken into account. Let alone if there are ten or 20 per cent of such soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Now, if we look at page 3 of this document, I won't mention the names of people who made these comments, just in order to preserve some confidentiality. We see reference there to clashes among the people in the army authorities, police. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you understand from this meeting and also from other information when were you in Tuzla, that there was in Srebrenica at this time at least three entities, the army, the authorities, the police, and that there were clashes among them and power struggles?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, last time I had said that I became corps commander just 20 days before the interview. What Mr. Jones is saying is exactly how it was. This is how I took it. I wanted to provide as much information as possible about that territory or my area of responsibility. That was only 100 kilometres away. I wanted to find out how I could affect the situation in order to improve things, to improve Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the atmosphere, and this is exactly how I took what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And your information included, didn't it, that Naser Oric and Zulfo Tursunovic, were in a conflict, that there was a clash between them?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard from Mr. Ken Biser. I heard about the conflict between the police, or rather these three entities, civilian authorities, army and police. That was the topic of the conversation. And when Mr. Ken Biser asked to meet with me as a commander, this is what we discussed. We did not go into details, and I asked him to verify all that information and to provide it to me later. We did not elaborate on any of those conflicts. I didn't know any of these people. I have only heard about Naser Oric but have never seen him before. The same goes for Hakija Meholjic. I didn't know any president of a municipality. They perhaps knew about me but I didn't know them. And I have lived in Tuzla for 28 years. However, when the new government came, I wasn't present and that's how this came about. I personally didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Finally on this document, and I'm looking at -- in the English it's the bottom of page 3 where there is reference to the food problems, that there are attempts to bring food in from Zepa, it says ambushed, several smugglers were killed, wounded, were put in the Srebrenica hospital. Two of the killed ones were 13 years old. Did you understand from this and from other information that even then in December 1994, there were still grave problems with food and people smuggling food, including 13-year-olds, were getting ambushed by the Serbs and killed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's definitely how it was, Mr. Jones. That situation existed in Tuzla as well, and it was a much-larger liberated area than Srebrenica, and in such a limited area, that was definitely even more so. This is the kinds of problems that the inhabitants faced.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm about to move to a new exhibits and a new area. So it probably is a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you wish, Mr. Jones. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Can I mention two matters briefly? One is just during the break I did have a word with my learned friend and it was the reference to booty as set out in a brochure and what was included in that that I was asking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Secondly, I think if I go quickly, I can probably be finished in 15 to 20 minutes. I know we are all keen to finish with this witness today. On the other hand if it looks like he's going to be coming ban tomorrow I would prefer to take my time. So it depends a bit on the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have some questions ourselves but I wouldn't imagine -- and what -- how much time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have a few topics but I won't be lengthy, not at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll try -- yeah, but again, how much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ten minutes, and you have 15, 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: 20 minutes maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: General, I would be grateful if you would look at a new exhibit we are going to pass up. The ERN number is 01824931 to 01824958 and this transcript of the meeting of the 292nd session of the RBH Presidency on the 11th of August 1995. And to go straight to the important parts, we see on page 2 of the English and the B/C/S that a Durakovic refers to visiting commander Delic in Tuzla. Firstly do you see that and secondly do you agree that that would be a reference to you? It's on the --

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall that Mr. Durakovic, and I think I'm correct in saying it's Nijaz Durakovic, visited you in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall but as far as I can remember, he wasn't by himself. He was accompanied by some members of the War Presidency, and I believe Mrs. Tatjana Ljujic-Mijatovic was a part of the delegation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in order for this to be clear, there is a reference to Delic in these minutes. Given this is a meeting of the RBL Presidency, do you agree that that would probably be Rasim Delic, Supreme Commander of the ABiH, and not you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I would have to go through the contents and then I could be more precise. I cannot be certain. I can presume that it did concern Mr. Rasim Delic as the commander of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. In itself it's not -- it's not terribly important. What I want to direct you to, and this is a discussion among other things of the fall of Srebrenica and the somber question of how many people were killed. And I'd like you to look at what the president of the Presidency, President Alija Izetbegovic, says about the situation as it had been in Srebrenica, and it's page 4 of the English and also page 4 in the B/C/S. It's actually 01824953 in the top right-hand corner. I won't ask you to read the whole thing because obviously that will take sometime. I'd like to direct your attention to the following passage in the second paragraph. It starts by saying, it's about a dozen or so lines down, "The problem was the relation between the civilian and military authorities. There were clashes between them. We tried to resolve this. It went so far that one or two men were killed in those clashes. Furthermore the civilian authorities, there was collaboration with the other side." And we see as it goes on that it's referring to Srebrenica. My question is this: Would it be right to understand from this passage that the president of the RBH Presidency was saying that in Srebrenica the civilian and military authorities were distinct from each other, that they clashed with each other, and that as for the civilian authorities, there was at least some collaboration with the Serbs? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could conclude that from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that also information which you received in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the same information from Mr. Ken Biser. Of course, as it was stated in the original, without any additional explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And then President Izetbegovic goes on to talk about propaganda by Milosevic's supporters, and he says "the propaganda was very strong, often there was starvation, then a convoy comes and there is a little food, then starvation again for 15 to 20 days, so there were high and low tides in that respect and the mood changed accordingly. Naturally there was propaganda." Have you seen that passage in the Bosnian? It followed from the --

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you direct me as to the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's page 4 still, it's the passage which follows the passage we just saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Page 4, and if you look in the top right-hand corner it should be 01824951.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 54, yes, tape 6-1, if that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you take the document you have, and you turn -- my apologies actually, maybe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's page -- my apologies, it's 4954, correct. And it says at the top, [B/C/S spoken] and then about 15 lines down, you see it says, [B/C/S spoken]. You see that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just read to yourself that -- that sentence, referring to starvation and then propaganda. My question is just this: Do you recall that there was very strong Serb propaganda at the time regarding the situation in Srebrenica? When I say at the time, I'm referring to -- referring to the whole period in fact from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could say so. And not only the propaganda but they even used poison gas and they tried to prevent the salt arriving from Srebrenica and to cause the shortage of iodine and they were trying to put forth the information that that part will go to Serbia anyhow, that it was given away as part of the arrangements and that the people shouldn't actually fight but rather leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you referred to attempts to prevent salt arriving, and I think it's probably iodine, did you see that as deliberate attempts to destabilise in effect the mental health of the population? Is that what you were getting at?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And isn't it right that there was a lot of Serb propaganda against Naser Oric personally?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe one could make such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would you agree that the Serbs hated Oric, if I can put it in those terms, because he fought back against the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we have an enclave which is 100 kilometres away from the free territory which they couldn't actually deal with and be rid of, then I would say that your conclusion is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, what I meant is he was resented for fighting back, rather than surrendering.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I believe that you are mistaken, then. They disliked everyone who was not a Serb, and they disliked everyone who was not in favour of Greater Serbia. That would include a child or my elderly parents who were completely unfit for war but they were killed nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to what Delic there says, and it's page 5 of the English. If you could turn to 4955 in the Bosnian. And it's a description of how things worked or did not work in Srebrenica. And you see there, if you see the passage which starts off, [B/C/S spoken]. Do you see that? In English, "We did what we could. Now it turns out that command and control do not function in this unit. They close the commander. They said you're going to be an intelligence operative as of tomorrow. The thing is that they are still at the year 1992 level." Now my question, then, if we can take this shortly, you were in Tuzla during this time. Can you explain how you understand that comment referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I object to the question, if Your Honours please. If there is any -- either the document speaks clearly to us from the face of the document, the words themselves, or if there is any confusion about it, only Mr. Delic, not this witness, can tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this witness is being asked what he understands from this comment here. What's wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the other Mr. Delic who said these words allegedly knows precisely what he had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it doesn't -- it doesn't mean that any other person reading this cannot try to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Any other person such as yourselves will have to read it and try to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is what the witness is being asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If there any ambiguity about what is written there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is suggesting that there is ambiguity?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's based on what the witness knows from being in Tuzla, from being a commander. Obviously it's not just what any of us might make of those words. Based on his experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's the person who is best placed from all of us here, with perhaps the exception of the accused, who was in a position to understand that three- or four-line paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him explain it or how he understands it at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, if you could go ahead, general, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is precisely as it is stated. The command and control system was not functioning, and we concluded that as part of our analysis of the genocide against the people of Srebrenica that was conducted after July 1995, and I believe to the large extent the situation was as it is stated and that's why Mr. Rasim Delic, who was the commander of the General Staff, ordered that a group of officers be flown by helicopter out of Srebrenica in order to train them on how the system should function within the enclave, and I would agree with what my commander stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I can move to page 7 of the English, you see General Delic and I think it's accepted now that that is Rasim Delic, referring to a "Naser Horic" as it is written?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a mistake in -- let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we are happy for that to be Naser Oric. And he's describing his position, quote, "However, my information now when he came here and when the army came he did not have much influence on his brigade as a commander. He was not a commander who had command over the situation in the division. He had command over his own brigade and another one. He had no influence over the others. So the level of military organisation in this area was low. We tried to bring as much influence to bear as we could in writing, by orders, and summoning all commanders. Regretfully, it did not work." So I think there might be a problem with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since the witness has the Bosnian original, it was misinterpreted to him when it was said that the level of education was very high instead of very low. So I'm kindly asking the general to verify against the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is page 6/4 or, rather, page 01824957, if that is the comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. And I think message received and the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. My question is this: Wasn't that also the information you received in Tuzla that from the start of the war, right through to 1995, that the level of military organisation in Srebrenica was low and that there was this lack of influence, lack of command, on the part of the commander?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can comment this from two points of view. There is a sentence by Mr. Zulfo Tursunovic that we discussed about breaking of the siege of Srebrenica. He said that he could live over a month in Srebrenica and that he didn't decide to go, and this is a very telling statement. It is my opinion that the local commanders had the necessary influence on -- over their units and that they decided what and how will happen, but I will decline to comment because I really don't know the extent of influence of Brigadier Naser Oric. I would presume that he did have some influence with some people, not all, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number for this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become Defence Exhibit D300.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Since we are running short on time I just have two areas I want to deal with as quickly as possible. First, can the witness please be shown P233? This is another subject altogether. And perhaps I can even -- I'll ask the witness to look at the document but I might be able to cut it short by asking this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you agree that in Tuzla, there was a Srebrenica TO in exile, if you like, in other words, a sort of Territorial Defence Staff calling itself the Srebrenica TO staff but which was actually physically in Tuzla in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there were some other municipalities with similar examples, such as Zvornik and Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So whether we see on I believe it's page 2 of the English, in any event, "commanding cadre of Srebrenica Territorial Defence in Tuzla," those people, Gadzo, Hadzo, and others, those officers were in fact based in Tuzla and receiving orders and communicating as the TO staff Srebrenica. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you to be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the real situation was, but reading this document I think you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll direct you to page 3 of the document you have, and you'll see a stamp on a hand written page. You need to turn it, I think sideways, and it says "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, District Staff, Territorial Defence, Tuzla." Do you see that stamp, in the bottom left-hand corner of the third page?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Does that confirm to you the communication which went between the Srebrenica TO Staff which was based in Tuzla and the Tuzla District Staff?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This stamp on the left side of the document bearing page number 01828367 says that the District Staff of Territorial Defence in Tuzla received the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I have four final questions. I trust Your Honours will indulge me. Firstly, general, you've described how you were very young, 35 years old, to be in such a position of influence. You agreed that Naser Oric was made a brigadier in 1994. You'd agree that he was in fact just 27 years old when he was made a brigadier in 1994.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in the former JNA, to be a brigade commander under the age of 40 would be impossible, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, all of my marks and grades were excellent, and yet I was promoted only twice, and in 1992 I was supposed to reach the level of brigade commander, but -- and still I was at least four to five years younger than my peers at that level so one would have to have at least 30 -- 40 to 45 years' experience to become a brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then finally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 40 to 45 years of age, not experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So to be a brigadier at the age of 27 would be extraordinary?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It only happens in a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally, you told us how you had regular meetings with Naser Oric in 1995, you said nearly every day. We have one final exhibit which we would like to pass up. And just to explain, it's from the United Nations Detention Unit in response to our letter dated 4th of May 2005. I'd ask you just to have a look and tell me if you agree -- look at the last page actually which is the Bosnian, very last page, whether you agree from your encounters with Naser Oric that his height was as recorded there, 180 centimetres or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thereabouts, yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would agree that when you knew Naser Oric, he didn't have blue eyes?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he doesn't have them even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we'd ask for an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be D301.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. Mr. Di Fazio, re-examination, please. And try to leave us a little bit of time for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: To become a brigadier at the age of 27, given all of the evidence that you have just moments ago told us about, regarding career paths, you would normally expect that to occur only in a man of some considerable talent, wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, Your Honours, I have a comment. The ranks were not assigned based on intelligence or the necessary skills and training. They were assigned based on the position held by the person at the time when the rank was assigned. Therefore, there were some illogical situations. For example, a former JNA colonel who is above a brigadier was in the position of a major or lieutenant colonel which was lower than the rank previously held by him in the former JNA. Therefore, to conclude, the ranks were assigned based on the establishment position and those who did not have appropriate professional skill would be assigned a rank one step lower. So, for example, the person who held a position of a general would be assigned a rank of a brigadier. So the ranks were not assigned based on professional skills, education, and particular military talents but, rather, based on the establishment position that was in force at the time. What was important was the position held by a person and not their skills, abilities, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do I take it that you can't tell us what particular skills or lack of skills or what particular attributes the 27-year-old Mr. Oric had that resulted in his appointment to the rank of brigadier?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Di Fazio. I personally believe that what I told you reflects the actual situation, meaning that regardless of skills and military education, if a person held a position of a commander of a municipal staff, then that person would receive a certain rank. For example, I was assigned a rank of a brigadier general, which was one step above than what I held previously. So when it comes not just to Mr. Oric but to myself and anybody else, the position was the only thing that mattered. Had I, for example, held a position within the Federation army, I would have been assigned a rank of general immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fine. You said -- you were asked some questions about Serb Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. propaganda, and it was suggested to you, probably quite accurately, that the Serbs hated Mr. Oric. You recall those questions a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if the Serb propaganda commented on the position, the role, of Mr. Oric in Srebrenica in that time that you heard any Serb propaganda?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe it or not, this is something for Mr. Ripley, but there is a stream in Tuzla running through Tuzla called Jala and it was rumoured that there were Serb corpses flowing down that stream and the stream is so shallow that it wouldn't carry a sheet of paper. That's how shallow it was. And this just shows how bad the propaganda was, especially when it comes to senior commanders, officers, or persons that they could not deal with. I'm sure that you have documents confirming this. You can find them in the media. It would be sufficient just to take and analyse the newspaper articles. Goebbels was an incompetent compared to their propaganda. You know that they had TV and radio transmitters under their control. The whole system was in their hands and they could do whatever they wanted to do in relation to the international community as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood me. I understand all of what you say and I'm not asking you to tell us everything that the Serb propaganda did and everything that they said about Mr. Oric. What I'm asking you is simply this: In the course of what you heard of Serb propaganda about Mr. Oric, did they ever present him as holding or having a particular position within the Srebrenica enclave? I don't want to hear everything chapter and verse but just about what the Serb perception of him was, what he was doing there, who he was and what he was doing there, his role?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, it's changed to the Serb perception. We were talking about propaganda a moment ago and think he just stated "perception.".

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: As expressed in the propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, you're right, Mr. Jones. But I think the question is clear enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've told you, Your Honours, during my previous testimony that I didn't have much time to follow the propaganda and all the rest. Everything that was said was phrased -- put in darkest terms. They threw flyers from the planes and did various things aimed at lowering the morale of the civilians and the army. Now, I couldn't tell you the exact stories that were rumoured about Naser Oric, but I can tell you that there were rumours about all of us and that they were very strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll leave that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown D297, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've already looked at this document. And under paragraph 2 of the document, it says that the Ministry of Defence shall assign senior officers to commands and the staffs of these units and will issue detail -- more detailed orders. Presumably, then, the Ministry of Defence was going to -- or as it says on the face of the document issue more orders in respect of these particular TO units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, in Bosnian language, in my native language, it appears that something else is stated here and that your translation is not all right. This is the decision on establishing Territorial Defence units, and on the last page, under item 14, the following is stated, at least in my language: "Minister of Defence shall assign senior officers to commands and the staffs of said units, and shall issue more detailed orders on the strength and weapons assigned to the formed units." This is what is stated in the original, in my language.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Perhaps we'll just move to other parts of the document. If you look at the document, is there any way it purports to provide an exhaustive list of Territorial Defence units that are to be formed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he answered that question earlier. He said this is limited to Zenica, Sarajevo, and incidentally includes also Srebrenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If that's the case of the evidence then that's entirely the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said it. You can go into the transcript and this is how he started it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fine. In that case I've finished with the document. Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment? I do apologise. If Your Honours would give me just one more moment. I may be able to avoid asking the questions that I wanted to, or that I thought I needed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were asked -- you were asked by Mr. Jones, wasn't the information that you received in Tuzla that right from the start of the war, right through to 1995, that the level of military organisation in Srebrenica was low and that there was a lack of influence, lack of command, on the part of the commander? You then went on to say, it is -- you then spoke about speaking to Mr. Zulfo Tursunovic. You discussed breaking the siege of Srebrenica. He said that he could leave over a month in -- live over a month in Srebrenica and that he didn't decide to go. Then you said it is my opinion that the local commanders had the necessary influence on -- over that -- their units and that they decided what and how will happen. But I will decline to comment because I really don't know the extent of influence of Brigadier Naser Oric. I would presume that he did have some influence with some people, not all, though. And I assume when you said some people you were talking about commanders. How do you reconcile that answer with your evidence in chief that at the very end of your evidence in chief, where you said that you had -- you were unable to comment on the relationships between individuals and entities in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just had one point and perhaps it is in effect the question that is being asked but Mr. Di Fazio decided to presume that it referred to commanders. Well, it didn't. He said that -- "influence with some people," so I see no warrant for that presumption. He didn't speak about Mr. Oric's influence over other commanders. Over some people. As far as the question is concerned you think it can remain but I think it needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough but I think the witness can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You understand my question, general?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I understood the question of Mr. Di Fazio. During my previous testimony I clearly stated that in 1992 through 1994, that's a period of time that I'm less familiar with, less than an ordinary citizen. That's what I stated. My first information about Srebrenica and the situation there were a result of the conversation I had with Mr. Ken Biser. Naturally, the stories that were second-hand or third-hand and so on were not that significant. I was quite frank and I gave you my position. However, that doesn't mean that that was necessarily true. It was a lie to say that Mr. Oric had no influence over anybody there. I think that Mr. Oric was a person who had influence over part of the population and part of the commanders, especially in 1994 and 1995, when in Srebrenica there was an attempt to establish and round off the system. At the end of 1994, a reorganisation of the BH army was conducted, including Srebrenica. The broader area of Srebrenica, where some reorganisation was done and some where some light brigades were established, numbering 900 to 1200 people. That was done somewhere on paper only and somewhere in reality. I just gave you an example of a commander which was affected by the lack of action on the part of the international community, and prompted by the situation in Srebrenica, he decided to leave it. If I were to tell you that I learned about their movement -- direction of movement only four days after they had set out, they -- the original intention was for them to go from Srebrenica to Zepa, which was much more favourable in military terms, the original idea was not for them to go to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further questions, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Brydensholt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: I understand that in Tuzla you had a prison where civilian and military prisoners were kept. I understand also that you, in the same prison, would have some prisoners of war. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in Tuzla, there was a military prison, as well as a civilian one. However, I have to tell you that in 1992, my soldiers were in the same prison as the captured enemy soldiers because that was the only facility that we had and sometimes they were even placed in the same room. However, as the time passed, we separated the facilities and then we had a military prison and a civilian one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Did you ever inspect, you in person ever inspect the military prison where the prisoners of war were also kept?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a book detailing that inspection. I visited the prison only two to three times, three times at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Were there any other officers, military officers, who were obliged to inspect this military prison, as part of their duty?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in Tuzla, for example, the Military Police Battalion was there in the military prison and elsewhere, naturally, during those periods of times when those civilians were under the jurisdiction of the military command. Later on, when they were turned over to civilian authorities, they were not in the hands of the army any more and the army did not decide their fate any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Eser?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I just follow up with this problem of military police? We saw a document, it has been shown to you, it was P123, where we have seen that two district defence staffs, Tuzla and Lukavac, had a military police company. There is no mention of other places where you had a military police company. Now, what does it mean? For instance, if there had been suspicions that certain violations of the law happened, who would report this or where could this be reported, or to put the question different: If there was no special military police company, would that mean that you would not be obliged to report at all? Or if you have to report, to whom and by whom?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, a consequence of such a situation was chaos that existed on the ground. I told you on Friday that my commander, my Supreme Commander, commander of the General Staff, General Halilovic, was never in Tuzla. He never communicated with me, even when I was the corps commander and commander of the operative group. That means that all locations organised themselves to the best of their abilities. To answer your question specifically, a unit was supposed to take action if the violations were made by their soldiers and if they had the ability to do so. If there was no military police, then I could have ordered a commander to take action. However, once the military police was established, the jurisdiction became clearly divided in certain fields under its jurisdiction. Therefore, what you are asking me is a result of the situation on the ground. I definitely myself committed an offence when, for example, I did not have a protection company, and I needed to have it. The person above me didn't know that I needed to have it. They thought that the system was well organised and was functionally properly; however, that wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Another question with regard to the Territorial Defence. I must say it's still a little bit unclear to me.
